title: Why crowds don't help, or do they?

lines.text: You've probably heard that people in a crowd won't help you. That might be wrong.
The idea is called the bystander effect. The more people watching, the less likely anyone helps.
It became famous after a 1964 murder in New York, where 38 people supposedly watched and did nothing.
But that story was exaggerated. There were far fewer witnesses, and police were called.
Lab studies still found an effect. In one, 70% of people alone helped, compared to 40% when paired with a stranger.
Then in 2019, researchers studied real CCTV footage of 219 street fights.
Bystanders stepped in over 90% of the time.
And the more people were around, the more likely someone helped.
So maybe people are braver than the textbooks say.

sources.claim: Kitty Genovese story exaggerated: far fewer than 38 witnesses, police called; NYT called its reporting flawed in 2016
Latané and Rodin (1969): 70% helped alone vs 40% with a stranger
Philpot et al. (2019): 219 CCTV-recorded conflicts; bystanders intervened in over 90%, more likely with more bystanders
